html:
On 5 August 2019 the government of India ended the special status of Jammu and Kashmir and split the state into two territories run from Delhi.

When Kashmir's ruler joined India in 1947 he handed over only defence, foreign affairs and communications (see the Kashmir conflict). Article 370 of the Constitution wrote this in. The state had its own constitution and flag, and Indian laws applied only with its consent. A linked rule let only permanent residents own land there. Over the decades Delhi wore much of this self-rule away, but the article stood. Hindu nationalists had wanted it gone since the 1950s; India's only Muslim-majority state, they said, must be like any other.

After winning re-election, the government of Narendra Modi acted without warning. Tens of thousands of extra troops were sent in first. Phone lines and the internet were cut, and thousands were detained, among them three former chief ministers. A presidential order and a vote in Parliament did the rest. Ladakh became a separate territory.

Mobile internet stayed slow or off for eighteen months. Pakistan cut trade and sent home India's ambassador.

In 2023 the Supreme Court ruled the change lawful and ordered elections, which were held in 2024. The promise to make Jammu and Kashmir a state again has not yet been kept.
sum: On 5 August 2019 the government of India ended the special status of Jammu and Kashmir and split the state into two territories run from Delhi.
